analysis.body:
# AI Adoption in Nonprofits

The nonprofit sector has begun adopting AI tools, though at a measured pace. According to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 12.6% of firms in the nonprofit-heavy "Other services" category (NAICS 81, which includes grantmaking and civic organizations) reported using AI in the two weeks prior to the survey, up from 11.3% in the prior period. This gradual increase suggests cautious experimentation rather than wholesale transformation, even as the sector grapples with longstanding resource constraints and operational pressures.

AI deployment in nonprofits centers on organizational effectiveness and trust-building rather than on the cutting edge of technical capability. Candid emphasizes that AI literacy is becoming a fundamental leadership skill for nonprofits, and that responsible AI policies and practices are essential to building trust with donors, grantees, and communities. The Center for Effective Philanthropy documents how foundations and nonprofits are navigating these tools amid historic challenges, signaling that AI adoption is tied closely to operational survival and funder expectations rather than competitive advantage. NTEN underscores that nonprofits view technology—including AI—through an equity lens, with a sector-wide commitment to ensuring equitable use, funding, and creation of tools rather than adopting AI for its own sake.

The nonprofit AI landscape remains fragmented and underfunded relative to commercial sectors. Only four individually verified organizations appear in the inventory of nonprofits and open-source foundations stewarding AI-related models, standards, and shared infrastructure, and none operate as compute or power infrastructure builders. LMSYS operates Chatbot Arena for benchmarking models, Khan Academy deploys AI for educational delivery, and organizations like Blender and Krita steward creative tools intersecting with AI-generated content, but their primary missions and funding predate AI. This indicates that AI development for nonprofits is not concentrated in nonprofit-led technical efforts but rather depends on tools built by commercial vendors and adapted for mission-driven use.

The sector faces a critical access and equity gap that vendors and funders have begun to recognize but not yet systematically address. The AI Equity Project works to make AI accessible and practical for underrepresented communities, building learning pathways and partnering with public libraries, yet this work sits at the margins of nonprofit technology adoption rather than at its center. NTEN's emphasis on dismantling inequities within nonprofit organizations and the sector suggests that many nonprofits lack the technical capacity, training, and governance infrastructure to deploy AI safely and in alignment with their values, even as adoption pressure from funders and competition for donors grows.

Organizations considering AI adoption should recognize that the sector lacks standardized guidance and that responsible implementation—not speed—is the defining concern. Candid and the Center for Effective Philanthropy both flag that AI governance, literacy, and ethical practice matter more to nonprofit stakeholders than technical sophistication. Nonprofits should approach adoption with attention to equity, staff training, and stakeholder trust, and should be aware that the sector's fragmented AI landscape means that off-the-shelf tools built for other sectors may not align with nonprofit values or capacity, and that infrastructure support remains sparse.
